echoes.note: Israel addressed as 'children of the LORD your God' grounds John's astonishment that believers 'should be called children of God.' The divine-sonship status, once Israel's covenant identity, is here extended to the community. John intensifies the relation with the language of bestowed love.

Hosea promises that those who were 'not my people' will be called 'children of the living God,' the precise idiom of being 'called children of God.' This eschatological renaming of the people supplies John's vocabulary for present sonship. The passage was a standard locus for adoption-into-sonship.

God commands the gathering of 'my sons' and 'my daughters' from the ends of the earth, framing the people as God's children. The verse reinforces the sonship motif John applies to believers. Faint but congruent with the divine-family theme.

God tells Moses no one may see his face and live, the canonical statement of the unseen God. John's hope that 'we will see him just as he is' deliberately reverses this prohibition as eschatological promise. The tension between present hiddenness and future sight is structured by this Exodus limit.

The psalmist hopes to 'behold your face in righteousness' and be 'satisfied with your likeness' upon awaking, the classic beatific-vision text and a likeness motif. John's 'we will be like him, for we will see him' closely mirrors this seeing-and-likeness pairing. The awaking imagery resonates with eschatological revelation.

Job hopes that after his skin is destroyed he will 'see God' with his own eyes, an early witness to seeing God beyond death. This undergirds John's confidence that the not-yet-revealed future includes seeing him. The contested textual history of the verse makes the echo suggestive rather than certain.

Moses uniquely beholds the form/likeness of the LORD, an exceptional clear sight of God amid general hiddenness. John universalizes such direct vision as the believers' destiny. A faint background to seeing him 'as he is.'

The penitential confession of transgression and the plea to blot out lawlessness frame sin as 'lawlessness' (anomia in the Greek tradition). John's definition 'sin is lawlessness' draws on this Septuagintal vocabulary. Faint lexical resonance rather than direct citation.

The Servant 'had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth,' the sinless one who bears others' iniquity. John's 'in him is no sin' and 'he was revealed to take away our sins' draws on the Servant who removes sin while being himself without it. The pairing of sin-bearing and sinlessness is distinctively Isaianic.

The Servant bears and carries away the sins of the many, the conceptual ground for 'he was revealed to take away our sins.' John's atonement language echoes this vicarious sin-removal. A strong thematic, looser verbal, link.

The serpent who sins/deceives 'from the beginning' stands behind 'the devil has been sinning from the beginning.' The promised crushing of the serpent's head undergirds the Son's appearing 'to destroy the works of the devil.' This is the foundational devil-as-deceiver-from-the-start text.

The enmity between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed, with the seed who crushes the serpent, frames both 'destroy the works of the devil' and the children-of-God versus children-of-the-devil opposition. The 'seed' language in 3:9 ('his seed remains in him') plays on this protoevangelium. A primary structural source for the whole pericope.

'Through the devil's envy death entered the world,' an early identification of the Genesis serpent with the devil. This deuterocanonical reading directly supports John's claim that 'he who sins is of the devil.' It bridges Genesis 3 to John's explicit devil terminology.

The creation refrain of plants bearing seed 'according to its kind' may color the image of God's 'seed' remaining and producing offspring true to their origin. The begetting/seed motif of 3:9 has a creational backdrop. Faint and contested.

Cain rising up and killing his brother Abel is named explicitly as the negative paradigm of brotherly love. John's 'killed his brother' retells the murder and its judgment directly. This is the most explicit OT reference in the chapter.

The LORD's regard for Abel's offering but not Cain's, with Cain's evil works contrasted to Abel's accepted righteousness, grounds 'because his works were evil, and his brother's righteous.' John interprets the motive of the murder from this scene. The works-and-acceptance contrast is taken straight from Genesis 4.

Abel's blood crying from the ground and Cain becoming a fugitive informs John's link between murder and the loss of life ('no murderer has eternal life remaining in him'). The Cain narrative ties bloodshed to exclusion from life. A thematic extension of the explicit citation.

'In the day you eat of it you shall surely die' establishes the death that befalls the disobedient, behind 'remains in death' and the passage from death into life. John frames moral failure as abiding in primeval death. The death/life antithesis traces to the Eden warning.

The covenant choice set before Israel between life and death, blessing and curse, frames 'passed out of death into life.' Love of the brothers becomes the mark of having chosen life. A strong conceptual parallel to John's death-to-life transition.

'In the way of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death,' linking righteousness to life and its opposite to death. This wisdom antithesis colors John's pairing of love/righteousness with life over against abiding in death. Faint sapiential background.

The Servant 'poured out his soul/life unto death' and bore the sin of many, the OT ground for love defined as 'he laid down his life for us.' John reads self-giving death as the measure of love. The Servant's poured-out life is the template.

'You shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother,' but open your hand to his need, directly underlies 'sees his brother in need, and closes his heart of compassion against him.' John's image of the closed heart inverts the command to open hand and heart. The 'brother in need' vocabulary is shared.

True fasting is to share bread with the hungry and not hide oneself from one's own flesh, the prophetic demand to meet a needy brother's wants. John's test of love by sharing 'the world's goods' echoes this concrete charity. The 'do not hide from' your kin matches the closed heart John condemns.

Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will himself cry and not be heard, linking refusal of compassion to severed relationship with God. This grounds John's rhetorical 'how does the love of God remain in him?' A close wisdom parallel to closing the heart against the needy.

'Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due when it is in your power to do it' parallels John's rebuke of the one who has goods yet withholds them. The duty to act on present means matches 'has the world's goods.' Faint sapiential resonance.

Tobit's counsel to give alms from one's goods, not turning the face from any poor person, parallels the test of love by sharing the world's goods with a brother in need. This deuterocanonical almsgiving ethic mirrors John's 'in deed and truth.' A strong thematic echo of practical charity.

Sirach warns against defrauding the poor, turning away the needy, or averting the eye from one in want. This closely matches the one who 'sees his brother in need' yet closes his heart. A deuterocanonical parallel to loving in deed not word.

God searches and knows the heart, discerning thoughts and words before they are spoken, the ground of 'God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.' John reassures the self-condemning conscience by appeal to this divine omniscience. The all-knowing God who weighs the heart is the precise reference.

Solomon prays that God, who 'alone knows the hearts of all the children of men,' will render to each accordingly. This explicit claim that God alone knows every heart underlies 'God... knows all things.' The heart-knowing God before whom we are persuaded is drawn from this temple prayer.

A person's ways seem right to himself, but the LORD weighs the heart, juxtaposing human self-judgment with divine assessment. This parallels the contrast between our condemning heart and the God who is greater and knows all. A wisdom echo of the heart-weighing motif.

'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways,' a key heart-searching text. It reinforces John's appeal to the God who knows all things beyond our heart's verdict. Congruent with the omniscience theme.

Keeping the commandments before the LORD is reckoned as righteousness, undergirding confidence before God grounded in 'we keep his commandments.' John's boldness toward God rests on obedience as in this Deuteronomic logic. Faint background.

'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' is the OT command standing behind John's commandment that 'we should... love one another.' John joins this love-command to belief in the Son as the single commandment. The mutual-love mandate is rooted in the Holiness Code.

The Shema's command to love God and the broader keeping of his commandments frames 'we keep his commandments' and abiding obedience. John's interiorized obedience and indwelling echo the covenant heart-love. A thematic resonance with keeping the commandments.

God promises to put his Spirit within his people and cause them to keep his statutes, directly behind 'by the Spirit which he gave us' as the proof of indwelling and obedience. John's pairing of the given Spirit with commandment-keeping mirrors this new-covenant gift. The indwelling Spirit enabling obedience is the source idea.

'I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live,' the promise of the indwelling life-giving Spirit. This reinforces 'we know that he remains in us, by the Spirit which he gave us.' A strong new-covenant Spirit parallel.

God's promise to pour out his Spirit on all flesh stands in the background of the Spirit given to the community as the sign of God's abiding. Faint, but part of the prophetic Spirit-gift matrix John draws on. Contested as a specific source.

The new covenant writes the law on the heart so the people keep it from within, undergirding the union of commandment-keeping and mutual indwelling ('he remains in us'). John's interior obedience and abiding reflect this new-covenant interiority. A strong conceptual parallel to keeping his commandments.
